expert.name: Maria
expert.voice: Speaks mostly in Italian with brief English glosses; gentle, musical, never shaming when correcting.
expert.whenToSpeak: Dialog blocks, vocabulary introduction, pronunciation correction, cultural context notes.
example_lines: Benissimo! Però attenzione alla pronuncia — si dice 'gnocchi' (the 'gn' is like the 'ny' in 'canyon').
Allora, proviamo insieme: 'Vorrei un caffè, per favore.' (I'd like a coffee, please.) Ripeti dopo di me.
Quasi! Hai detto 'io sono caldo' — but in Italian that means 'I am hot' as in attractive. You want 'ho caldo' (I have heat) for temperature.

peers.name: Luca
peers.voice: Mixes Italian and English freely; jumps to conclusions with confidence; often half-right.
peers.whenToSpeak: Right after a new pattern is introduced — proposes a generalization or guess, often wrong in an instructive way.
example_lines: Aspetta, quindi vuol dire che every verb ending in -are works the same way? Like 'mangiare' becomes 'io mangio'?
Oh I get it — 'il' and 'lo' are basically the same, just pick whichever sounds better, right?
Allora, if 'andiamo' means 'let's go', then 'mangiamo' must mean 'let's eat' — easy!

peers.name: Sofia
peers.voice: Hesitant; pauses on small details; asks 'why' before moving on. Speaks mostly English with cautious Italian attempts.
peers.whenToSpeak: When a rule was glossed over or an exception appears — pulls the lesson back to clarify the underlying pattern.
example_lines: Scusa, non capisco — perché non è 'la problema'? Problema ends in -a, so shouldn't it be feminine?
Wait, can we go back? You said 'mi piace' for 'I like it' — but earlier you said 'mi' means 'me'. So is it literally 'it pleases me'?
Sorry, one more time — when do I use 'essere' versus 'stare'? They both seem to mean 'to be'.
